Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failure stems from how FastDateFormat handles a Calendar whose fields were explicitly set in one time zone and then formatted in another.

- The test builds a GregorianCalendar in GMT-8, clears it, and sets the fields (year, month, day, hour, minute, second). At this point the calendar has its “fields” set, but its internal time computation may be deferred.
- FastDateFormat.getInstance("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'", GMT) returns a formatter with mTimeZoneForced = true.
- When formatting, FastDateFormat.format(Calendar) delegates to format(Calendar, StringBuffer). In that method:
  - If mTimeZoneForced is true, it clones the input Calendar and calls calendar.setTimeZone(mTimeZone) to switch it to GMT.
  - It then immediately calls applyRules to read the calendar fields and build the output string.
- Due to a known JDK quirk, calling Calendar.setTimeZone on a calendar whose fields were manually set does not force an immediate recomputation of those fields for the new time zone. Unless you force a recomputation (e.g., by calling calendar.getTime() or similar), subsequent field reads (Calendar.YEAR, HOUR_OF_DAY, etc.) can return values that still reflect the old time zone’s local fields.
- FastDateFormat.applyRules iterates rules that read calendar fields directly, so it formats the “stale” field values from GMT-8 rather than the recomputed ones for GMT. As a result, the hour stays at 08 instead of converting to 16, causing the assertion to fail.
- This matches the current bug report: changing the Calendar time zone during formatting can leave fields inconsistent unless a recomputation is triggered. The fix is to force recomputation after setTimeZone (e.g., by calling calendar.getTime()) before applying rules.
